Replace each sub-expression that you are not manipulating with a symbol that stands for it.
Keep a sub-expression written out only on the line where you are about to apply its definition, a rule or a theorem to it.
Every other line shows the symbol.

This is one case of [making each expression as concise as possible](#making-expressions-concise).
It also asks for the habit behind that advice:
split a long expression into short named pieces,
and give each piece the symbol or [shared macro](#using-shared-macros) that names its concept.

Choose the symbol to match the thing it names.
For the population mean $\E{X}$, write $\mu$.
Add a subscript, such as $\mu_X$, only when the context holds a second mean and the reader could confuse the two.
State the abstraction once, in a sentence such as "Let $\mu = \E{X}$",
before the first line that uses the symbol.

::: {#exm-abstract-unused-subexpressions}

## Abstracting the population mean

Suppose a derivation expands the variance of a random variable $X$.

> ❌
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \E{\paren{X - \E{X}}^2}
> &= \E{X^2 - 2 X \E{X} + \E{X}^2}\\
> &= \E{X^2} - 2 \E{X} \E{X} + \E{X}^2
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> ✅ Let $\mu = \E{X}$.
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \E{\paren{X - \mu}^2}
> &= \E{X^2 - 2 \mu X + \mu^2}
> && \text{(expand the square)}\\
> &= \E{X^2} - 2 \mu \E{X} + \mu^2
> && \text{(linearity of expectation)}\\
> &= \E{X^2} - 2 \mu \mu + \mu^2
> && \text{(definition of } \mu \text{)}\\
> &= \E{X^2} - \mu^2
> && \text{(combine like terms)}
> \end{aligned}
> $$

In the ❌ version, $\E{X}$ is a constant that no step manipulates until the last one,
yet it clutters every line.
In the ✅ version, only the line that uses the definition of $\mu$ needs to know what $\mu$ stands for.

:::
